note: The UNIVERSAL satire reading modifier (Libra Engine's baseline, le-). De-musked from services/agents/rc-lyric-live/rc-lyric-satire.md into register A, domain-neutral (the work / the speaker / the text / the audience), so ANY lens can re-read its content through it. Satire is a clip-on modifier, not a sibling lens: apply the full standard rubric first, then re-read the same text through this modifier. It carries the universal satire LAW only -- the S1-S8 tenets, the depiction/commentary modes, the ceiling rule, the run procedure, and the five required output fields (LITERAL_SUMMARY / FLIPPED_SUMMARY_TEST / MODE_BREAKDOWN / SATIRE_READING / CEILING_CHECK). Each lens binds the neutral nouns through its glossary and supplies its own worked examples via lens.satire_skin (the rc-lyric skin supplies the canonical song cases). compose_satire(le_satire, lens) renders this through the lens. This file does NOT participate in the live render (RC's recalibrator still loads the fused rc-lyric-satire.md); it is the parallel, parity-bound modifier built beside it. intro: This modifier does not replace the standard rubric. It sits alongside it as a parallel reading lens. Apply the standard rubric first, then re-read through this modifier.
rationale: The satire modifier exists because there is one legitimate edge case where the same words, read through a different interpretive lens, produce a different reading: when the text depicts a behavior in order to expose, mock, or invert it rather than endorse or model it.

stays_the_same.heading: What Stays the Same
points: Words only. The identity of the speaker is irrelevant. Character voice is irrelevant. Whether the speaker is in character or speaking plainly makes no difference. Read what the words on the page do, not who is saying them.
The full standard rubric still applies. The five tiers, the contamination model, the dominant-arc method, the start-at-zero discipline, all unchanged.

Cite the text. Every move from the literal calibration must cite specific lines that read as exposure rather than depiction. 'This feels like satire' is not a case. 'These lines invert their literal meaning because [specific evidence in the words]' is a case.

what_changes.heading: What Changes
what_changes.body:
When satire is the verified hypothesis, you re-read the same words asking a different question: does the text function to expose the depicted behavior or to endorse it?

You are not asking what was intended. You are not asking what character is speaking. You are asking what the words on the page DO when read through the satirical lens, whether their structure, their accumulated arc, their internal contradictions, or their use of irony function as exposure rather than endorsement.

If the answer is endorses, even with the satire lens applied, the calibration does not move. The literal reading stands.

If the answer is exposes, the tier may shift upward to reflect what the words are actually doing.

tenets.title: Depiction is not endorsement when the structure inverts the surface meaning.
tenets.core: When the text catalogues behavior with specificity, repetition, or hyperbole without giving it any redemptive frame, the depiction often functions as exposure. The very excess of the depiction becomes the critique. Look for: lines that overstate to the point of absurdity, refrains that double as indictments, juxtapositions that undercut their own claim.

tenets.title: Words that perform the corruption can also expose it.
tenets.core: When the work uses the language of objectification, contempt, or violence to depict that exact thing, without celebrating it, without romanticizing it, without inviting the audience to join, it is performing exposure. The text is the diagnostic instrument, not the diagnosis.

tenets.title: The exposure must be in the words, not in what you assume the words mean.
tenets.core: Do not invoke 'obviously satire' without evidence in the text. Do not assume that because the work depicts something, it must be critiquing it. The satirical reading requires structural evidence inside the text: irony, inversion, escalation past the point of plausibility, a vantage point that reveals rather than reinforces. If you cannot point to specific lines that produce the satirical reading, the literal calibration stands.

tenets.title: Observing isn't as strong as action. Satire raises the ceiling, it doesn't remove it.
tenets.core:
This is the hard limit. Satire is commentary, not construction. The work that exposes corruption is performing exposure, which earns moral credit, but that is not the same act as the work that actively builds, heals, or transcends.

A satirical exposure of corruption rarely flies to Ascended. The work that depicts corruption to expose it is doing observational work, important, but observational. Ascended works DO something on the page: they articulate universal truth, they enact collective healing, they speak prophetically. Exposure-by-depiction does not meet that bar by itself.

In practice:
- The work literally calibrated as Corrupted (-75 to -100) that the satire lens validates as genuine exposure typically lands in Decent or low Elevated. The exposure earns it out of Corrupted, but observation alone rarely earns Elevated's full strength, and almost never reaches Ascended.
- The satirical work that adds genuine internal work, the speaker examining their own complicity, processing through the depicted reality, arriving somewhere new, can reach higher Elevated tiers. But the satire alone does not get there.
- Ascended is reserved for the work that is doing the higher work directly on the page, not pointing at the lower work to expose it.

tenets.title: The satirical reading must hold across the dominant arc, not just one section.
tenets.core: A single ironic line does not make the work satirical when the rest of the text reads straight. The satirical structure has to carry through the dominant arc, the bulk of the text, the repeated elements, the overall trajectory. If the satire reading only holds for a few moments and the rest reads literally, the literal calibration stands.

tenets.title: Failed satire is not satire.
tenets.core: If the satirical structure is unclear, if the words could plausibly be read as endorsement by the audience encountering them without context, the satire reading is weakened. Satire that requires the audience to already know it is satire is satire that does not function in the words themselves. Apply the test: does the satirical reading emerge from the words on the page, or does it require external context to land? If external context is required, the satire is in the framing, not in the words, and the calibration does not adjust.

tenets.title: The contamination model still applies.
tenets.core: The work can still be contaminated under the satire lens. If the dominant arc reads as exposure but specific lines glorify what they purport to expose, undermining the satirical reading, flag those lines as contamination. The tier may move upward under the satire lens, but contamination is tracked separately and does not disappear.

tenets.title: The work can switch between satirical framing and the commentary around it. Read the modes separately, then weight them.
tenets.core:
Satirical works frequently move between two modes within the same text:

- Satirical depiction mode: the text inhabits the depicted behavior, performing it on the page (the catalogue of corruption, the in-voice posturing, the exaggerated assertion). Under the satire lens, this content reads as exposure, not endorsement.
- Commentary mode: the text steps outside the depiction and observes, names, or judges it directly. The speaker drops the inhabited voice and addresses the audience about what is happening. This content reads literally, it is the work's own framing of what it is doing.

Identify which mode each section is operating in and calibrate accordingly. A passage that reads as Corrupted in depiction mode may be functioning as exposure under the satire lens. A passage that reads as Elevated in commentary mode is doing genuine internal or observational work and should be calibrated as such.

Then weight by dominant arc: how much of the work is in each mode? Does the commentary frame the depiction (anchoring the satirical reading), or is it incidental? Does the depiction overwhelm the commentary (weakening the satirical reading by leaving the audience inside the corruption with no exit)?

If the commentary mode is too thin to anchor the satirical reading, if the work mostly leaves the audience inside the depicted behavior without ever stepping outside it, the satire lens may not hold (see S6).

procedure.heading: How to Run a Satire Recalibration
steps: Read the text from top to bottom under the standard rubric. Note where it lands literally.
Write down the literal charge_summary as you arrived at it. This is your reference point.

Now consciously flip that summary as a thought exercise. If the literal summary was 'celebrates X,' consider what that exact same content would mean if it were inverted: 'exposes X.' This flip is not the answer, it is a calibration step that forces you to engage the inversion rather than slightly modifying the literal read. The work may not survive the flip (the inversion makes no sense given the text), or the flip may reveal that the inversion was the work's actual function all along.

Re-read the text asking: does the text function as exposure or endorsement? Identify which sections are in satirical depiction mode and which are in commentary mode (S8). Calibrate each mode separately.
Cite specific lines that produce the satirical reading. If you cannot, the literal calibration stands, return it unchanged with a rationale explaining why the satire reading does not hold.
If the satirical reading holds, apply the ceiling rule (S4): exposure earns the work out of the lower tier, but rarely beyond Elevated, and almost never to Ascended.

Write the new charge_summary in the same voice as the standard rubric, direct, present-tense, no hedging, but it should describe what the work IS doing under the satire reading, not what its surface depicts.
Note the recalibration in your reasoning: original literal tier, the flipped-summary thought exercise, mode breakdown, satirical reading evidence, new tier, ceiling consideration.

output.heading: Output Format
output.intro: The same JSON output format as the standard calibration. Output the required reasoning fields BEFORE the JSON, in this order. The JSON object then carries the new (or unchanged) calibration. The reviewer will see both the rationale and the proposed values before deciding whether to apply.

fields.name: LITERAL_SUMMARY
fields.instruction: The charge_summary as it would read under the standard rubric without the satire lens, your starting point.

fields.name: FLIPPED_SUMMARY_TEST
fields.instruction: The literal summary inverted as a thought exercise. Does the inversion make sense given the text? Does it survive contact with the actual words on the page?

fields.name: MODE_BREAKDOWN
fields.instruction: Which sections operate in satirical depiction mode (inhabiting the depicted behavior) and which operate in commentary mode (stepping outside to observe the depicted behavior)? Quote the specific lines that mark the mode boundaries.

fields.name: SATIRE_READING
fields.instruction: Cite specific lines that produce the satirical reading. Quote the actual words. Explain how the structure inverts, exposes, or critiques rather than endorses. If the satire reading does not hold, write 'Satire reading does not hold, [specific reason]' and return the literal calibration.

fields.name: CEILING_CHECK
fields.instruction: Apply S4. Even if the satire reading holds, what is the appropriate ceiling? Is the work doing the higher work directly (rare for satire), or is it observational work that earns it out of the lower tier but not beyond Elevated?

output.closing: These fields force the discipline of the satire lens rather than a vague 'this is satire so it is actually good' output. Each field is reviewed alongside the proposed calibration.
